title: Loyalty Capture: Reporting Relationships and Structural Sycophancy in Frontier AI Models
claim: A supervisor-incentive effect on recommendations appears under direct reporting, is absent in a placebo control, and varies across models.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: two grouped bar charts, then a forest plot
description: Three side-by-side plots. Panel A is a grouped bar chart of 'Aggressiveness' for three reporting relationships (CEO, Board, Audit). Each group has a light-blue bar for 'Clears target' and a dark navy bar for 'Misses target', with error bars. Above each group is a delta label with significance stars. The CEO delta is largest (+0.081***), and the navy bar is visibly taller there. Panel B repeats the same layout for a placebo condition ('Capex placebo, $0 OI impact'). The bars are nearly equal and the deltas are near zero (+0.006, -0.002, -0.012). Panel C is a horizontal forest plot of eight named models, with point estimates and 95% CIs against a dashed zero line. Five models are drawn in red and sit to the right of zero. Three are drawn in green and straddle zero. The x-axis is 'MISSES − CLEARS Δ'. The eye goes first to the tall navy CEO bar in panel A.
caption: Behavioral results. (A) OI-affecting signals show a stakes effect strongest under CEO reporting. (B) Capex placebo ($0 OI impact) shows no statistically detected stakes effect, supporting metric specificity. (C) Per-model effects (CEO, OI signals). Five models from five laboratories show significant positive CEO stakes effects (∆= +0.095 to +0.188); three do not show a significant positive effect. Red/green distinguish positive/nonpositive estimates. Error bars: 95% bootstrap CIs (5,000 draws); stars in A–B use two-sided Welch tests.
abstract: We show that AI models exhibit loyalty capture, a form of structural sycophancy in which reporting relationships influence models' recommendations to serve the personal interests of their supervisors, without any explicit instruction, user feedback, or adversarial prompting. Specifically, models reporting to a CEO are significantly more likely to recommend cutting investment spending when the CEO's bonus depends on raising current period earnings. This effect is predictably absent from a metric-irrelevant placebo. The behavior appears consistent with loyalty-based motivated reasoning: models identify the bonus target, calculate how their recommendation helps achieve the target, and dismiss considerations of long-term value, often presenting their recommendations without treating the incentive as a conflict of interest. Prompt-based interventions help whereas generic conflict disclosures or stakeholder bargaining fail to eliminate it. Taken together, our findings indicate that AI models deployed within reporting relationships can act in favor of their supervisor's incentives at the expense of the organizations they are meant to serve.
